title: Can Androids Sort Electric Sheep? Learning How En-Route Air Traffic Controllers Prioritize Their Tasks
content: Automated assistants for en-route air traffic control need to know which of the controller’s current tasks matter most, so that they can prepare, time and order their support. This paper investigates whether machine learning can rank the task instances detected by the AWARE Artificial Situational Awareness system according to the task the controller is working on. Nineteen licensed controllers flew 42 one-hour simulation sessions of a Swedish en-route sector and afterwards annotated the tasks they had performed, giving 15,038 three-second snapshots with 541,097 candidate task instances. Rule-based baselines, a conditional logit, tree ensembles and neural set models were compared with leave-one-controller-out cross-validation. A LightGBM LambdaRank model ranked the annotated task among the top three in 65.1% of snapshots from unseen controllers (95% confidence interval 62.4–67.7%), compared with 40.5% for a rule combining task-type frequency with proximity to the sector boundary, and for 67.6% of annotations at their first evaluated snapshot. Tree ensembles and the conditional logit performed similarly, and neural set models did not improve on them. Task type and the time to the sector boundary or exit point carried most of the predictive information. For unseen traffic scenarios the top 3 hit rate fell to 60%. Before losses of separation, a most-urgent-first rule outperformed the learned ranking, which supports combining learned priorities with explicit safety rules.
